Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Desmond Holt is a 60-year-old warehouse worker of British descent who has been in a relationship with his partner of eleven years. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 62, seeking help for the first time regarding experiences that have their roots in his military service nearly four decades ago, though he describes the past two years as a period in which something has shifted, and the weight he has carried quietly for so long has become impossible to manage alone.

Desmond served in the infantry during a period of active combat deployment in his late twenties. During one particular engagement, his unit came under sustained and unexpected fire in a narrow clearing. In the chaos that followed, several of his fellow soldiers were killed within yards of him. Desmond was wearing standard-issue combat fatigues - the rough texture of the collar, the particular weight of the fabric across his shoulders - when he watched men he had known for years die in a matter of minutes. He survived, largely by chance of position. He has never fully accepted that distinction between luck and deserving.

In the years immediately following his discharge, Desmond managed to build a functional life. He found work in logistics and warehousing, married briefly, and eventually settled into his current relationship. He did not speak about what had happened, and for a long time the silence felt like containment. He had come to believe that as long as he did not look directly at the memory, it would remain at a manageable distance. He stopped visiting the town in the south where he had been stationed for training before deployment - a place he had once known well - and he stopped wearing any clothing that resembled military-style garments. These were not decisions he announced; they were quiet rearrangements of his life that accumulated over years. His partner noticed that he refused to wear the olive-green work jacket she bought him one winter, but he offered no explanation she found satisfying.

At the warehouse where he works, Desmond operates a forklift on the floor of a large industrial space. The environment is loud, physically demanding, and populated almost entirely by younger men. On one occasion roughly two years ago, a colleague arrived wearing a surplus military jacket - the kind sold at army disposal stores - and something in the cut of the collar and the dull green of the fabric stopped Desmond mid-movement. What followed was not a flashback in the cinematic sense, but a flooding of terror so complete and so immediate that he was certain, in that moment, that he was back in the clearing. The terror did not feel like a memory. It felt like the present tense. He had to leave the floor and sit in his car for forty minutes before he could return to work. He told no one what had happened.

Since then, when he tries to recall the event in any deliberate way, the same terror returns with an intensity that feels indistinguishable from the original experience. Alongside it comes guilt - a guilt he cannot reason his way out of, a certainty that the men who died deserved to live more than he did, that his survival was not neutral but was somehow taken from them. What frightens him most is that he cannot articulate any of this clearly. He knows what happened. He can sequence the events. But when he tries to put the experience into words - with his partner, in the single conversation they have attempted, or now in the intake session - he reaches for language and finds nothing adequate. The sentences stop before they carry any weight.

He has come to feel that the man he is now bears little relationship to the man he believed himself to be. He describes this not dramatically but with a flat bewilderment, as though he has misplaced something essential and cannot remember where he last saw it. He is also increasingly convinced that the world is a place in which catastrophe is always proximate, always possible.

What finally brought Desmond to seek help was his partner's quiet statement that she felt she was losing him. He came not because he believes he can be helped, but because he does not want to lose her too.
